transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2028-06-18
- Start time (UTC): 16:00
- Duration: 48 minutes (recording)
- Attendees: Avery Moore (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lena Park (CTO, Navigator Labs), Jonah Reed (Sr. ML Eng), Marta Li (Infra Lead)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on where Navigator Labs should host embeddings/rerank inference (hosted vs dedicated vs private), expected throughput (peak ~60k qps for embedding lookups, 4k rerank requests/min), current vector DB topology, shard counts, and data residency/SOC2 constraints. Redwood AE/SE outlined cost/latency tradeoffs, KV/prefix caching, quantized model options and fallback routing for hybrid search. Action items and a perf-deep-dive were agreed.

Topics covered:
- Current vector DB characteristics and constraints
- Embedding dimensionality & candidate recall vs latency
- Rerank flow: where to run heavy scoring (hosted vs dedicated CPU/GPU)
- Throughput scaling, sharding, and cold-cache tails
- Security: VPC, KMS, audit logs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery Moore: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — uh — we'll kick off. I'm Avery from Redwood, AE, with Diego our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Lena Park: Doing well, thanks. Jonah's got some numbers to share. Marta is on for infra questions.
[00:11] Jonah Reed: Yep, morning, thanks. We're, uh, excited to talk through tradeoffs.
[00:15] Diego Ramos: Cool. Quick agenda: we'll run through your current stack, expected QPS and latency targets, then map hosting options. Does that work?
[00:22] Lena Park: Sounds good. Quick context: Navigator Labs runs a product search where we embed product text and user queries; we store vectors in a managed VDB and then do a 128-dim cosine topK, then send top 50 to a reranker.
[00:35] Jonah Reed: Right now our vector DB is sharded across 6 nodes, each node about 12m vectors, average vector dim 128, using an IVF+PQ index. We get about 8k search qps sustained, spikes to ~60k during promotions.
[00:48] Marta Li: And we have strict controls: SOC2 required, customer data residency in EU, VPC peering only with approved vendors.
[00:55] Avery Moore: Great, that's helpful. When you say rerank — is that a full transformer-based reranker per query? Latency target there?
[01:02] Jonah Reed: We do a distilled cross-encoder for rerank, roughly 2.4B param model, runs on GPU right now. Target p95 latency for rerank is sub-1200ms, ideally under 800ms for interactive features.
[01:15] Diego Ramos: Okay, so two pieces: embedding search (vector DB) and the rerank stage. For the embedding side we often recommend a cache-first approach for hot keys and to keep fanout low. For rerank, dedicated GPUs or Redwood Dedicated makes sense if you need predictable tail latency.
[01:30] Lena Park: What does cache-first look like in practice? Is that something Redwood handles or we implement?
[01:36] Diego Ramos: Redwood can do prefix/KV caching at the runtime — we keep the KV cache local to the serving node and can serve many rerank KV hits without touching the model. But for closed-loop candidate scoring you still might need full model runs for cold candidates.
[01:50] Jonah Reed: There's also a cost question: hosting on Redwood hosted API vs dedicated capacity vs our own private deployment. We need rough unit economics.
[01:58] Avery Moore: Absolutely. We can model per-token and per-embedding cost. For embeddings at 128 dims, cost per-embedding is usually low; the bigger driver is rerank model cost and GPU-milliseconds. We'll put together a tailored cost-throughput spreadsheet.
[02:13] Marta Li: Important: any hosted solution must support VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for key rotation.
[02:20] Diego Ramos: We support VPC options on Private and Dedicated; hosted has private endpoints and the hosted VPC peer option — but if you need full customer-managed KMS and air-gap, Private is the path.
[02:30] Lena Park: How do you handle fallback if capacity is maxed during spikes? We can't have user-facing errors.
[02:35] Avery Moore: Redwood has policy-based routing and automatic fallback to cheaper model variants or queued bursts. For retrieval you can also fallback to cached results or increase similarity threshold to reduce candidate set.
[02:47] Jonah Reed: When you say cheaper model variants, are we talking quantized cross-encoder or smaller dense models?
[02:52] Diego Ramos: Both. We often run 8-bit quantized variants of the reranker for heavy load, and keep a full-precision variant on warm nodes. There's a small quality delta; we can show eval tolerances on your prompt set.
[03:05] Lena Park: Curious about embedding dimensionality. Our team experimented with 384 dims but vector DB ops got heavier. Is 128 still OK for recall?
[03:12] Avery Moore: It depends on retrieval recall targets. For product search 128 often hits good recall if the embedding model is good; 384 gives headroom but increases index size and I/O. Diego, do we have rough disk/QPS multiples?
[03:22] Diego Ramos: Sure — roughly 3x storage and 2-2.5x search latency at similar node counts moving from 128->384, given same index type. But quality gain plateaus for some models beyond 256. Jonah, you mentioned IVF+PQ — PQ compression changes the math a bit.
[03:36] Jonah Reed: We're already using PQ with 8 bits per subvector, but recall drops on tail queries sometimes. We're exploring hybrid recall: ANN topK=200 then rerank top50.
[03:46] Marta Li: From infra perspective, we prefer not to run heavy rerank on the DB nodes; keep inference separate.
[03:51] Diego Ramos: That's typical — separate serving layer for rerank. Redwood Dedicated can colocate GPU pools and do consistent throughput. For burst protection we can have a spillover to hosted region if private is saturated (subject to compliance).
[04:05] Lena Park: Can you describe autoscaling behavior for dedicated pools? How fast can you get more capacity?
[04:10] Avery Moore: Autoscaling is policy-driven. For Dedicated you can configure burst capacity that spins up additional reserved nodes — warm-up is about X minutes (we'll capture exact numbers). For Private on-prem, scaling is manual unless you integrate with your cluster autoscaler.
[04:23] Jonah Reed: What's X minutes? Our promo spikes can start and end inside 10-15 minute windows.
[04:28] Diego Ramos: For cloud-backed Dedicated, warm-up to usable capacity is typically 3-7 minutes for hot GPUs with prewarmed images; full steady-state might be ~10-12 minutes. For really tight windows we recommend combin ing caching and a modest buffer of reserved capacity.
[04:45] Marta Li: We're exploring a hybrid approach: embeddings and nearest neighbor search in our managed VDB (Milvus currently) within our VPC, but rerank in Redwood Dedicated to minimize infra changes. Is that supported?
[04:56] Avery Moore: Yes. Many customers keep their VDB and use Redwood as the inference tier. We integrate via private endpoints and can pull vectors/payloads or accept topK ids and fetch from your VDB — several ingestion patterns.
[05:08] Jonah Reed: Any latency hit when fetching payloads from our VDB into Redwood rerank? We're sensitive to tail p95.
[05:14] Diego Ramos: Network hop adds ms. If you colocate Redwood Dedicated in same AZ and VPC peering is in place, the fetch is sub-10-20ms typically. If you stream payloads in the same request path it can be negligible. We'll capture network diagrams.
[05:28] Lena Park: How do you recommend we measure quality vs cost? We want to avoid big regressions when we quantize.
[05:33] Avery Moore: Redwood Optimize can run prompt-set-based evals comparing model variants (quantized vs full) and show quality curves. We also tie alerts to regression thresholds.
[05:42] Jonah Reed: Good. Can you run an eval on our rerank prompt set? We have 500 queries labeled.
[05:48] Avery Moore: Absolutely. Diego — we'll need a snapshot of their dataset and the labelling schema.
[05:53] Diego Ramos: Noted. Also, Jonas — Jonah — how are you currently handling cold-cache tails for vector searches?
[05:59] Jonah Reed: We have a small LRU cache at the edge for top user intents, maybe 30k keys, but for big promo spikes that doesn't help.
[06:07] Diego Ramos: Those constraints make a case for more aggressive local KV caching at the inference tier and sharded hot partitions. We also recommend route-based throttling and graceful degradation — degrade rerank precision for non-logged-in users for example.
[06:20] Marta Li: Let's talk about observability. We need token-level and request-level cost breakdowns, traces across VDB->rerank.
[06:27] Avery Moore: Redwood Console exposes token and model-level cost attribution, per-route latency distributions, and traces with identifiers you can correlate with VDB traces. You can also export to your Datadog.
[06:38] Lena Park: On security, SOC2 + ISO and audit logs — we need to show auditors how keys rotate and that no vectors are stored outside region.
[06:47] Diego Ramos: For Private we can ensure customer-managed KMS and region-locking. For hosted we have region-restricted deployments and audit logs; we'll share SOC2 reports and the VPC architecture doc.
[06:58] Jonah Reed: Quick question: if we choose Dedicated but then want to move to Private later, how hard is that migration?
[07:04] Avery Moore: We designed it to be smooth — same API and model versioning. Migration is mostly network and KMS reconfiguration plus capacity provisioning. Usually weeks, not months, depending on on-prem procures.
[07:18] Lena Park: For our cost modeling, can you show the break-even threshold where Dedicated becomes cheaper than Hosted given our 60k spike profile and average daily qps 12k?
[07:27] Avery Moore: Yes — we'll run scenarios: sustained vs spiky, percent of queries hitting rerank, and percent of cached hits. Diego will prepare the matrix.
[07:36] Diego Ramos: I'll model 3 scenarios: 128-dim/384-dim and two rerank model sizes (distilled vs full cross-encoder) and show cost per successful rerank plus tail latencies.
[07:47] Jonah Reed: What's Redwood's support for model quantization toolchain? We do some in-house quant but want Redwood to validate.
[07:54] Diego Ramos: We support standard quant toolchains (8-bit, 4-bit experimental) and can run CI-style checks against your eval set. We'll surface quality deltas as part of Optimize.
[08:06] Marta Li: Operational question: how do you handle per-tenant isolation in Dedicated? We don't want noisy neighbor issues.
[08:12] Avery Moore: Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools per customer with configurable sharing policies. You get reserved instances and you can cap concurrency per model to protect SLAs.
[08:22] Lena Park: Can you do a quick sketch of an architecture that uses our Milvus VDB + Redwood Dedicated for rerank?
[08:28] Diego Ramos: Sure — (diego shares screen) diagram: user -> edge cache -> query to Milvus (VPC) -> topK ids -> Redwood rerank service in same VPC -> retrieve payloads via fast path -> rerank model (quantized fallback) -> response. We also have fallback to cached topK if redisbacked.
[08:50] Jonah Reed: That fast path — do you prefer fetching payloads inside the rerank request or prefetch into memory?
[08:56] Diego Ramos: Prefetching into memory on the inference node lowers tail variance. For big topK we stream and score progressively, but prefetching top50 is common.
[09:06] Marta Li: Any preference on batching? Our rerank QPS is bursty, so larger batch sizes reduce cost but increase latency.
[09:12] Diego Ramos: Redwood supports continuous batching with latency budgets. You can set SLOs and a maximum batching window; the runtime will batch within that budget to improve throughput.
[09:24] Lena Park: For our metrics, we're tracking MRR and NDCG on rerank outputs. Can you produce those in the Console?
[09:30] Avery Moore: Yes — we can ingest eval metrics and present per-model MRR/NDCG and link regressions to deployments.
[09:36] Jonah Reed: Let's talk numbers: rough config for rerank on Dedicated for our peak — how many RTX A100s or comparable GPUs?
[09:44] Diego Ramos: For a 2.4B cross-encoder, throughput per A100 with 8-bit quant might be X qps — (note: X is a placeholder we'll benchmark). Ballpark: 100-300 qps per GPU depending on batch and sequence lengths. For 4k rerank reqs/minute sustained (~67 qps) you'd need modest pool size but spikes to thousands require buffers + autoscaling.
[10:05] Jonah Reed: Ok, so for spikes to 4k/min (67 qps) it's fine, but 60k embedding lookups is the heavier piece at ANN layer.
[10:12] Avery Moore: Right — embeddings scale differently; embedding generation is typically per user input and is cheap relative to rerank compute, but search fanout and VDB IO is the heavy part.
[10:22] Marta Li: On the VDB side, what changes would you recommend to handle 60k spikes? More shards, or more nodes per shard?
[10:29] Diego Ramos: Increase node count and spread replicas, and use hot-partitioning for promo items. Might also use edge-level prefiltering to lower fanout. We'll recommend sharding maps based on your access patterns.
[10:41] Lena Park: Any gotchas with Milvus and Redwood integration?
[10:45] Diego Ramos: Mainly network topology, index parameter alignment, and consistent vector normalization. Also watch for metadata fetch times if payloads live in a separate DB.
[10:55] Jonah Reed: On the compliance side, will Redwood sign an SA? We need a DPA and include security appendix.
[11:00] Avery Moore: Yes — we have standard DPA + security addendum. We'll share legal docs and SOC2.
[11:06] Marta Li: We also need timeline: pilot -> eval -> procurement. We're aiming for pilot in Q3.
[11:12] Avery Moore: Sounds reasonable. Our typical pilot is 4-6 weeks including basic perf runs and an eval on your labeled set.
[11:19] Lena Park: One last technical item: tail latency budgeting for our rerank p95 under 1200ms — how does Redwood measure and enforce that?
[11:25] Diego Ramos: We measure per-request latencies end-to-end. Enforcement is via routing policies (cap concurrency per instance), warm reservoirs for hot keys, and fallback to quantized model variants if needed. We can also set circuit-breakers.
[11:38] Jonah Reed: If we do a pilot, what's the minimum telemetry and artifact access you need?
[11:43] Avery Moore: We'll need a sample of your vector/metadata pipeline, 500 labeled rerank queries (you mentioned), and access to a staging VPC or dataset to replicate tail patterns.
[11:52] Diego Ramos: Also your index parameters (nlist, nprobe, PQ config) and historical QPS traces.
[11:59] Lena Park: We'll share that.
[12:02] Avery Moore: Okay great — to recap next steps: we'll send the cost-throughput spreadsheet, SOC2 + VPC docs, and schedule a 2hr perf-deep-dive with Diego and your infra team.
[12:12] Jonah Reed: Thanks, appreciate it.
[12:15] Marta Li: Thanks everyone.
[12:17] Avery Moore: Thanks, we'll follow up with those materials and action items.

(There is occasional crosstalk and minor transcription artifacts. Some product names spelled differently by the transcription engine: 'Milvus' sometimes as 'Millvus', 'KV' transcribed as 'K V'.)
